newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, copper continue to rise, grains fall.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, copper continue to rise, grains fall.

text.p: Coffee prices continued to rise on Thursday as speculators pushed futures prices to new life-of-contract highs before profit-taking trimmed gains.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery rose as high as 265.00 cents a pound before easing back to close at 260.30 cents, up 7.20 cents.
The July contract was up almost 20 cents since Tuesday following expiration of the May futures contract, which set a 20-year high at 280.00 cents a pound last week.

The latest surge in prices was tied to news on Wednesday that coffee-producing nations would continuing to limit their coffee shipments to a set quota until July 1998, providing no increase in supply from the current year despite high prices.
But traders were also sensitive to daily weather forecasts for Brazil, the top producing nation, which is just entering its winter season when coffee trees face threats of frost.
"It was just an extension of yesterday's gains," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "And they may have priced in a potential weather problem."

Although forecasters said colder air is not now expected to damage Brazil's coffee trees, talk of temperatures dropping at a time when inventories hover near 20-year lows is likely to spark some panicky buying.

In a monthly bulletin, Brazilian independent forecasters Somar said two of Brazil's key coffee regions -- northern Sao Paulo state and southern Minas Gerais -- may see below average temperatures from now to July.
"This is due to the entry of cold air masses, which, together with clear skies (common in winter), favor low temperatures in the early mornings," Somar said.
Copper prices in New York continued to post gains, with futures posting life-of-contract highs for the third time in a week with prices now at their highest levels in almost a year.
Copper for July delivery at the COMEX closed at 118.95 cents a pound, up 0.75 cent.

"I am not, from these price levels, real bullish," said David Rinehimer of broker Smith Barney. "Fundamentally it's hard to see, in my opinion, prices going much above 120 cents without buying from China or disruption in supplies."
Warehouse stocks of copper continued to fall on good commercial demand, with jitters about strikes at Chilean copper mines also supportive to prices.
Sources said on Thursday that supervisors at Chilean state copper company Codelco's Chuquicamata pit are likely to accept the firm's pay offer in a vote next week and not go on strike.
Codelco is due to make its final offer Monday and around 700 supervisors will vote on the deal Tuesday. Chuquicamata's 7,000 miners went on strike for 10 days last year.
The mine, the largest of Codelco's four mining divisions, produced 632,000 metric tons of fine copper last year.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended little changed in quiet trade ahead of the Memorial Day weekend. Crude oil for July delivery ended unchanged at $21.86 a barrel.

Traders say the oil supplies are more than adequate but sellers of futures have been thwarted in part by nagging concerns about conflict in Iraq between Kurds in the north of the country and Turkish government forces.

"There are still background concerns about these political military cross-currents in northern Iraq. People are concerned that it could blow up into something serious," said Jim Ritterbusch, an trader at Sweeney Oil in Chicago.
Gasoline for July delivery closed 0.23 cent a gallon higher at 65.10 cents and July heating oil rose 0.17 cent a gallon to 57.85 cents.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices fell as excellent crop weather continued in the Midwest. Wheat for July delivery closed down 5 cents a bushel at $3.77-1/4, while July corn ended 3-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $2.73-1/4.
